content: An RNA virus is a type of virus that uses ribonucleic acid (RNA) as its genetic material and does not replicate through a DNA intermediate. These viruses are classified into Group III, Group IV, or Group V according to the Baltimore classification system. The RNA in these viruses is typically single-stranded (ssRNA) but can also be double-stranded (dsRNA). Examples of notable human pathogenic RNA viruses include SARS, Influenza, and Hepatitis C. Single-stranded RNA viruses can be further categorized based on the sense or polarity of their RNA into positive-sense, negative-sense, or ambisense RNA viruses. Positive-sense RNA is identical to viral messenger RNA (mRNA) and can be directly translated by the host cell. In contrast, negative-sense RNA is complementary to mRNA and must first be converted into positive-sense RNA by an RNA polymerase before translation can occur. Purified RNA from a positive-sense virus can directly cause infection, although it may be less infectious than the complete virus particle. However, purified RNA from a negative-sense virus is not infectious on its own, as it requires transcription into positive-sense RNA. Ambisense RNA viruses transcribe genes from both the positive and negative strands. Double-stranded RNA viruses represent a diverse group of viruses that infect a wide range of hosts, including humans, animals, plants, fungi, and bacteria. These viruses vary in the number of genome segments (ranging from one to twelve) and in the structural organization of their virions, such as capsid layers or turret structures. Notable members of this group include rotaviruses, which are the leading cause of gastroenteritis in young children worldwide, and bluetongue virus, an economically significant pathogen affecting cattle and sheep. Recent advancements have provided detailed atomic and subnanometric insights into the structures of key viral proteins and capsids of several dsRNA viruses, revealing significant similarities in their structural and replicative processes. RNA viruses generally exhibit high mutation rates because they lack DNA polymerases, which are capable of proofreading and repairing errors in genetic material. Consequently, RNA viruses are unable to perform DNA repair. In contrast, DNA viruses have much lower mutation rates due to the proofreading capabilities of DNA polymerases in the host cell. Retroviruses, which integrate a DNA intermediate of their RNA genome into the host genome, have a higher likelihood of correcting errors in their genome due to the proofreading activity of host DNA polymerases. Despite the rapid mutation rates typically associated with RNA, certain RNA viruses, such as the SARS virus, contain a gene that mutates very slowly. This gene has a complex three-dimensional structure, hypothesized to provide a critical chemical function necessary for viral propagation, potentially acting as a ribozyme. Mutations in this gene are likely to impair its function, preventing the virus from propagating. Animal RNA viruses can be categorized into four groups based on their replication strategies: 1. Positive-sense RNA viruses use their genome directly as mRNA, producing a single protein that is subsequently modified by host and viral proteins to generate the various proteins required for replication. One of these proteins is RNA replicase, which copies the viral RNA to form a double-stranded replicative intermediate. This intermediate then directs the synthesis of new virions. 2. Negative-sense RNA viruses require their genome to be copied by an RNA polymerase or transcriptase to produce positive-sense RNA. As a result, these viruses must carry an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase enzyme within their virion. The positive-sense RNA then serves as viral mRNA, which is translated into proteins by the host ribosomes. These proteins, including capsid proteins and RNA replicase, facilitate the synthesis of new negative-sense RNA molecules and the assembly of new virions. 3. Double-stranded RNA viruses, such as reoviruses, contain multiple RNA segments, each encoding an mRNA. These segments associate with proteins to form a single large complex, which is replicated using virally encoded replicase to produce new virions. 4. Retroviruses are single-stranded RNA viruses that replicate using a DNA intermediate. After the viral RNA is uncoated, a viral enzyme called reverse transcriptase converts the RNA into a complementary DNA strand, which is then copied to form a double-stranded DNA molecule. This DNA directs the synthesis of new virions.
